new_statements.quote: Kere has predictable stress, much like Hua (Haiman 1980). As mentioned above, stress in this language is indicated by vowel duration, and syllables with primary stress tend to be longer than others. [...] At the word level, primary stress is initial, while secondary stress is assigned to alternating syllables from left to right, as seen in the examples of disyllabic, trisyllabic, and polysyllabic words below. Suffixation changes stress patterns only when it changes the number of syllables in a word. [...] These words behave predictably based on their number of syllables, rather than on their number of morphemes, unlike Kuman (Hardie 2003).
new_statements.citation: Rarrick, Samantha Carol. 2017. A Tonal Grammar of Kere (Papuan) in Typological Perspective. PhD dissertation, University of Hawai'i at Manoa.
new_statements.locator: Section 2.2.1 'Stress', printed pp. 26-27 (PDF pp. 44-45); see also 2.2.2 'Rhythm' p. 29 and 3.3.7 'Tone and stress' pp. 112-114
new_statements.reading: tone language with a stress statement
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: File checked: (223 pp., Word-generated text layer; extracted text of PDF pp. 44-47 = printed pp. 26-29) plus the. Section 2.2.1 'Stress' opens on printed p. 26 exactly as quoted: "Languages of Papua New Guinea can have predictable or contrastive stress (Cahill 2011). Kere has predictable stress, much like Hua (Haiman 1980). As mentioned above, stress in this language is indicated by vowel duration, and syllables with primary stress tend to be longer than others." and on p. 27: "At the word level, primary stress is initial, while secondary stress is assigned to alternating syllables from left to right, as seen in the examples of disyllabic, trisyllabic, and polysyllabic words below…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is predictable and non-contrastive: primary stress on the first syllable of the (phonological) word, secondary stresses on every other syllable thereafter (left-to-right trochees), e.g. [ˈgil.suˌβɛ] 'pain', [ˈkɛb.naˌβa.i] 'younger sibling'. Stress is realised mainly as vowel duration; pitch is reserved for the independent lexical tone system (L/H), which does not directly interact with stress.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Secondary stress on alternating syllables after the initial, left to right (trochaic feet); a trisyllable gets secondary stress on its final syllable (degenerate foot), often repaired by medial vowel syncope; in compounds the non-head word takes secondary on its first syllable.
new_statements.exceptions: Proclitic subject pronoun + verb stressed as one word (primary on the pronoun); in compounds only one member keeps initial primary stress (choice predictable from foot count); phrase-initial monosyllables are demoted to secondary stress to avoid primary-primary clash; vowel syncope triggers re-footing.
new_statements.domain_note: Explicitly word-level rule (phonological word, including procliticised pronouns), with separate discussion of compound and phrasal stress/clash; measured from naturalistic narratives of two speakers (Praat durations). Kere is described as having contrastive lexical tone alongside this predictable stress.
new_statements.identity_note: The statement describes Kere, a variety of Sinasina spoken in Du, Silma, Mondia and neighbouring villages (Glottolog dialect kere1300 under sina1271; ISO sst). Rarrick treats 'Sinasina' as a district label covering several tok ples varieties (Kere, Tabare, Gunangi, Dinga, Nimai, Kebai, Kondo) that differ mainly in lexical tone patterns; the older grammar (McVinney & Luzbetak) describes the Tabare variety (taba1262).

sources.note: Sec. 2.2.1 (pp. 26-28): Kere has predictable stress cued by vowel duration (not pitch); primary stress word-initial, secondary stress on alternating syllables left-to-right (trochaic feet); suffixation changes stress only by changing syllable count; compounds/phrases show clash avoidance (phrase-initial monosyllables demoted to secondary). Sec. 3.3.7 (pp. 112-114): stress and lexical tone do not directly interact; High tone barred from initial (stressed) syllables of polysyllables. Language has contrastive lexical tone (ch. 3, Table 5 p. 154/180).
